Three steps from unboxing to a live display. You need a Raspberry Pi 5 (4 GB+), a microSD card and an HDMI screen.
Download the PitchTribe OS image and flash it with Raspberry Pi Imager. It bundles Raspberry Pi OS Lite, the PitchTribe stack and kiosk mode.

Open the dashboard on any phone, tablet or laptop on your club network. Update notices, menus and fixtures live — from the bar, the car park, wherever.

The software is. PitchTribe is MIT-licensed open source, with no subscriptions, per-screen licences or hidden fees. You pay for the hardware once, and for the electricity it uses — a Pi 5 draws a few watts, though the TV it drives will be the larger share.
Does it need an internet connection?
No. Displays and the dashboard work entirely over your local network. Internet is only needed for optional features like league fixture imports and software updates.
Can I run more than one screen?
Yes. Each Pi 5 drives up to two displays, and you can add as many Pis as you like — manage them all from one dashboard, each showing its own playlist.

The screen is nearly always the most expensive thing in a PitchTribe install, and it is the one thing the parts list above leaves out. So here is a small, honest selection. UK prices including VAT, checked 3 November 2026.

Those last two columns are the whole decision, and the gap is roughly £100 to £350 per screen. An ordinary smart TV is a television that happens to be showing a dashboard. A signage panel is a screen sold to be left on all day, in a room nobody is paid to watch.

PitchTribe draws large text, a crest and a results panel, read from three metres or more. At that distance 1080p and 4K are the same picture, and the 1080p screen is £50 to £90 cheaper. Spend the difference on a duty rating and on brightness instead.

A plate or bracket for the Pi itself
— the official case has no mounting holes
Match the bracket to the weight and the hole spacing, not to the inch rating.

Reckon on about 8 kg for a 43″ screen, 15 kg for a 55″ and 20 to 25 kg for a 65″, with signage panels a little heavier than televisions of the same size. The VESA hole pattern is printed in the manual and it is not always what the bracket box claims to cover.

And the failure nobody plans for: plasterboard with nothing solid behind it will not hold a 65″ screen on plasterboard plugs, however good the bracket is. That is the fixing, not the mount. Ten minutes with a stud detector before anyone drills is the cheapest part of the whole job. If the building is leased or listed and you are not allowed to drill at all, the floor stand or the trolley is the answer — worth knowing before you order a bracket.

A television is warranted for use in a home. A clubhouse is commercial premises and ten hours a day is commercial use, and manufacturers do turn claims down on exactly that basis. Signage panels are sold for the job and usually carry three years.

This is the one you will meet weekly. Televisions have eco timers and no-signal shutdown, and when power comes back they wake on the tuner rather than on HDMI. Somebody has to walk over with a remote. A signage panel wakes on the input you told it to and stays there.

The same header bar in the same place, all season. Signage panels shift their pixels slightly to cope with that and are rated for unchanging images; a cheap television left on one layout for a year can keep a ghost of it.
Brightness, if there is a window

Budget televisions run around 250 to 300 cd/m², which is fine on an inside wall. Facing a south-facing clubhouse window you want 500 cd/m² or more, and that is a high-brightness panel rather than a television at any price.

Only signage panels are rated to run portrait. A television mounted on its end traps its own heat and voids the warranty twice over, so if the wall you have is tall and narrow the choice is already made.
Budget smart televisions increasingly boot to their own launcher, with adverts on it, and some nag for a button press before they carry on. A signage panel has no tuner and nothing to sell you.

PitchTribe’s guest Wi-Fi runs on the Pi’s built-in radio, which covers about one room. For a clubhouse with a terrace, or a ground with a stand and a pitchside bar, add one of the two upgrades below. Guests get the same sign-in page, time limits and speed limits wherever they are, and you switch it all on from the dashboard. UK prices including VAT, checked 4 November 2026.
The Pi’s own radio. Fine for a bar or a small clubhouse with the Pi in the middle of it. Nothing to buy.
An Alfa Wi-Fi adapter with two screw-on aerials, on a short lead so it can sit high up and away from the TV. Reaches much further, through walls and out of a window, on 2.4 or 5 GHz.
Access points on the ceiling or an outside wall, cabled back to the Pi. Phones move between them without signing in again. The way to cover a stand, a function room and a pitchside bar at once.

Plug it into one of the Pi’s blue USB ports and PitchTribe uses it in place of the built-in radio, by itself. We chose Alfa’s AC1200 because its chip has worked as a hotspot in standard Linux for years — no extra drivers.
Alfa AWUS036ACM dual-band USB Wi-Fi adapter
Keep the extension lead to 2 or 3 metres; longer USB leads lose the connection. Point the aerials straight up, and put the adapter as high and as central as you can.
